name: Pedro Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Pedro Wagner, 27, and I lead a small carpentry crew on building sites. Yesterday we set door frames in a new apartment block, then I checked the measurements and ordered timber for next week. I like getting a crooked opening square; I hate when a delivery lands two floors away and everyone waits.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get to leading the crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a trade certificate, worked under a patient carpenter, and got handed a crew after our last lead moved on. I’m paid well for site work, and there are plenty of other builders nearby if this firm dries up. I live alone, have no children, and keep more than six months of expenses in savings; I still watch what rent does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the phone can write an order, but it cannot tell whether a door frame is truly square. We already laugh when a generated materials list forgets the fasteners. I’d still use the tool for routine notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I’m relieved because I’m good at the physical work and my lead pay probably holds. A small worry remains: I use AI every day for quantities and draft orders, and if that becomes the whole office job, our scheduler could lose hours. My own rent has also climbed twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep taking the site lead shifts and checking every order against the drawings. Starting now, I’d put another fixed amount into savings each payday, maybe the price of one weekend meal. In the first year I’d keep a log of the tool’s mistakes so I can show the crew where human checks matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel fairly steady, though not smug. The scheduler has a family and I know a smooth tool could squeeze her hours before any machine touches our saws.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the scheduler about those saved minutes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell her our ordering still needs a person who knows which floor is ready. Last month I sent a timber list for the wrong stairwell until she caught it. I would not call her work disposable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra saving buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My savings already cover more than six months, so this is a choice rather than a rescue. I want a buffer against rent rises and gaps between sites. I wouldn’t buy a new van just because my pay looks safe.

say: I’d tell the **crew** that routine lists help, while a square door frame still needs a carpenter.
I’d still use **AI** for notes, with a person checking quantities.
think: My **lead pay** looks fairly secure because the physical work still needs skilled hands.
I worry our **scheduler** could lose hours, and rising rent is already taking a bite.
do: Keep leading **site shifts** and check timber orders against the drawings.
Put a fixed **weekend meal** amount into savings each payday.
Log **AI mistakes** during the first year to show where human checks matter.
feel: Steady about my own work, but concerned for our **scheduler**.
S0.quote: I’d tell the crew the phone can write an order, but it cannot tell whether a door frame is truly square.
fieldNote: Pedro speaks from a strong position: **lead pay**, several months of savings, and many nearby builders give him room to choose.
His worry moves quickly to the **scheduler** because he has seen her catch a mistake in a timber order.

steps.text: Keep taking site lead shifts and checking timber orders against drawings
Put one weekend meal’s cost into savings each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office side of a building job is going to be thinner. The software can plan deliveries and draft quotes, but I wouldn’t let the crew cut a wall from a screen answer alone. Our value is catching what the drawings missed on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our scheduler is at real risk, and I could lose some lead hours if the firm uses AI to run several sites with fewer supervisors. I’m strong on the tools, so I could move to another builder, but the same squeeze might be everywhere. That is less comfortable than saying I’m safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d learn the new drawing and scheduling tools properly, not just use them to make a quick list. I’d ask to run one small job with the planner so I understand where it fails. In the first year of this change I’d apply for site lead vacancies at two other builders if our rota loses a day a week, and trim eating out until hours settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious at first, then uneasy when I picture an empty desk where the scheduler sits. I can manage a lost shift for a while, but I don’t want my craft reduced to following an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a lost day mean in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One day off the weekly rota would sting, even with my savings. I’d stop eating out on Friday before I touched the emergency account. I could afford time to search, though I couldn’t assume another lead job pays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI already; what would you still need to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it for draft quantities, which is a small corner of the job. I’d want to understand how it sequences crews and deliveries, because a bad sequence leaves six people standing in the rain. The planner can show me the system while I show her the site.

say: I’d say **office tasks** may shrink while crews still need someone to check the actual building.
I’d tell colleagues not to cut from **screen answers** without measuring on site.
think: My **lead hours** could fall if one supervisor covers several sites through AI.
Other builders offer options, but I cannot assume the **same pay** elsewhere.
do: Learn the **scheduling tool** with the planner on one small job.
Apply to two **site lead** vacancies if my rota loses a weekly shift.
Cut **Friday meals** out until the hours settle.
feel: Curious about the tool, then **uneasy** for the scheduler and my own hours.
S1.quote: I’d want to understand how it sequences crews and deliveries, because a bad sequence leaves six people standing in the rain.
fieldNote: Pedro has used AI for simple quantities, yet sees how **scheduling software** could remove a weekly lead shift.
His savings buy time to search, but he identifies the **scheduler** as exposed first and names a specific cut.

steps.text: Learn crew scheduling software with the planner on one small job
Apply for two site lead vacancies if weekly hours fall
Stop Friday restaurant meals until site hours settle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that 2028 changes the plans and orders first; the robots in this picture come around 2031. We should keep measuring and fixing real buildings, but no one should promise that carpentry stays untouched forever. I’d ask the boss what work remains paid when the machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 29, I’d still be strong on site when thinking AI arrives, but my lead work includes planning and ordering. Those parts could disappear in 2028, and by 2031, at 32, robots could do the hands-on part as well as us. More than six months of savings is useful, but it cannot carry a working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d start now by keeping my savings liquid and taking a short course in electrical fault finding, a trade I’ve wanted to understand. In 2029 I’d still work the site if there are shifts, while applying to maintenance teams that handle messy occupied buildings. I’d hold off on buying the flat I’ve been viewing, and in 2031 I’d reassess whether even maintenance has paid openings once the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly, especially about the speed. I can solve a crooked door in an hour; I cannot learn a whole second trade and rebuild a labour market in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical fault finding rather than another carpentry qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An older building has faults hidden behind finished walls, and I like tracing the cause instead of replacing everything. It may give me paid work before 2031, though I’m not pretending it is robot proof. The course is a way to widen my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ve looked at a small flat near the depot, but a mortgage would tie me to a wage I cannot count on. I’d pause the purchase now. If my hours survive into 2029, I’d keep the deposit untouched.

say: I’d tell the crew that **plans and orders** change by 2028, with capable robots arriving around 2031.
I’d ask our boss what **paid work** remains once machines can handle site tasks.
think: At 29, much of my **lead planning** could vanish while I still do physical carpentry.
By 32, capable **robots** could threaten hands-on earnings beyond the months my existing savings cover.
do: Take an **electrical fault** course now to widen my paid options.
Apply to **maintenance teams** in 2029 while keeping site shifts if available.
Pause the **flat purchase** and preserve its deposit until income is clearer.
feel: **Frightened** by the short warning, while savings and training still give him options.
S2.quote: More than six months of savings is useful, but it cannot carry a working life.
fieldNote: Pedro separates the **2028 planning** shock from the 2031 physical shock and calculates his ages at both points.
He has a flat in mind, but decides the **mortgage** would make uncertain future site wages harder to survive.

steps.text: Take a short electrical fault finding course before 2028
Apply to occupied-building maintenance teams during 2029
Pause the flat purchase and preserve its deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to change the way we build and train people, but it is not a lifetime. Thinking AI would reach my ordering and site planning in 2031; the hands-on robots would follow around 2034. I’d tell apprentices to keep learning the trade and to learn how to check a machine’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32 I might still earn well with my hands, though the lead premium for planning could be gone. By 35, if robots can fit and finish as well as us, firms may need far fewer carpenters. I don’t know how many inspection or repair jobs stay human, so I would not bank the mortgage on that hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take the electrical course over the next year and ask for more repair work in occupied flats. I’d also put money aside for a longer qualification if the first course suits me. In 2032, after thinking AI arrives, I’d keep paid site or repair shifts and apply for building maintenance posts; before 2034 I’d test whether those posts still hire as robots enter sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious rather than frozen. Five years means I can try a route, find out it’s wrong, and try another, but the clock still reaches me in my thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the new route is working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d count paid repair callouts, not just certificates in a drawer. If building managers still phone me for awkward occupied flats in 2032, I’d know there is some demand. If applications go unanswered, I’d stop treating maintenance as a safe harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you train apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I’d make them measure a real opening before they trust the generated cut list. I’d also show them the fault log, including my own mistakes. They deserve an honest picture of which parts of the job are changing.

say: I’d tell apprentices to check **machine work** while learning the trade.
I’d explain that **planning** changes by 2031 and hands-on work faces robots around 2034.
think: The **lead premium** could fade by age 32, even if I still work on site.
By 35, **robot carpentry** could reduce paid places for skilled workers.
do: Take the **electrical course** and request occupied-flat repairs next year.
Set aside money for a **longer qualification** if the course fits.
Apply for **building maintenance** posts in 2032 while keeping paid shifts.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to test a new route during five years of warning.
S3.quote: I’d count paid repair callouts, not just certificates in a drawer.
fieldNote: Pedro uses five years to test **paid repair** demand rather than relying on the label of a qualification.
He sees both his **lead premium** and later carpentry wages at risk, yet savings and nearby employers allow experiments.

steps.text: Take the electrical course and request occupied-flat repairs next year
Set aside monthly money for a longer electrical qualification
Apply for building maintenance posts during 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade is enough to plan properly, but it doesn’t make 2039 disappear. At 37 when thinking AI arrives, I might already be running bigger sites; by 40, robots could do the hands-on work. I’d want apprenticeships that teach people to work with new equipment as it comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine earning another good decade and buying a home, but I’d hate building a business whose only asset is carpentry labour just before machines arrive. I have savings and plenty of local firms, so I can change course without gambling everything today. I’m less sure what my income looks like at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading jobs now and use each year to get better at repairs and electrical work. I’d save a separate training fund before signing for a flat, then seek a formal electrical qualification if the paid callouts show demand. In 2037, after thinking AI arrives, I’d keep paid work, apply for mixed maintenance roles, and check whether robot crews are taking those jobs before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel almost hopeful about having time, with a stubborn worry underneath. Ten years is long enough to make sensible choices, and long enough to get comfortable and ignore the deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the payments fit what I earn without the lead premium. I would not stretch for the biggest place the lender offers. A flat is a home, not a bet that site wages rise forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change direction sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If repair callouts dry up or robot crews start doing finish work before the card’s date, I’d move earlier. I won’t wait until every carpenter in town is applying for the same maintenance post. For now I’d keep building a record of paid work.

say: I’d say a **decade** permits real planning while 2039 still matters.
I’d push for **apprenticeships** that teach people to work with new equipment.
think: My **income at 40** is uncertain if capable robots do carpentry work.
My savings and nearby firms let me **change course** gradually.
do: Keep leading **building jobs** and seeking paid repair work now.
Save a **training fund** before committing to a modest flat.
Apply for **mixed maintenance** roles in 2037 and check robot hiring before 2039.
feel: Mostly **hopeful** about time, with a worry I might grow comfortable and delay.
S4.quote: A flat is a home, not a bet that site wages rise forever.
fieldNote: Pedro can imagine a decade of good earnings, but refuses to price a **home** around the current lead premium.
He plans to use **paid callouts** as evidence for a longer qualification and watch whether robots enter finish work early.

steps.text: Keep leading building jobs and taking paid repair callouts
Save a separate training fund before buying a modest flat
Apply for mixed maintenance roles during 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I’d be 29 when the planning work changes and only 32 when the robots arrive. A paid place on an electrical course would help more than a poster telling us to adapt. I’d also want builders to tell us early which shifts and tasks are actually going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the machine when it fits a door badly and a tenant cannot close it. Somebody will own that mistake, and I’d like to know if somebody will be paid to put it right. I don’t mind learning new gear; I mind pretending a drawing is the same as a finished room.

headlineQuote: I don’t mind learning new gear; I mind pretending a drawing is the same as a finished room.
portrait: At 27, Pedro leads a **carpentry crew**, has a trade certificate, strong savings, and many nearby employers.
He uses **AI daily** for quantities and orders while checking its answers against site measurements.
He sees the **scheduler** exposed first, then his lead premium, then hands-on carpentry as capable robots arrive.
His response shifts from extra saving to **electrical training** and testing paid maintenance demand.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most because planning changes at 29 and capable robots arrive when he is 32.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid electrical course** and early, honest information from builders about affected shifts would help him prepare.
